scores.note: Strongest is Ijeoma refusing to file the one form on principle, which is a parent joke with a spine; weakest is that a stranger on the porch every 22 minutes reads as a sketch premise until the family story proves it can carry a week.

Strongest is a joke on every line of the pitch, from 'Objection, he's winning' to 'Court is adjourned, also dinner,' and both my kids would file suit by Saturday; weakest is that home-courtroom is a familiar sketch shape and kid cross-examination of a parent sits close to soft rule 2 every week.

Strongest is Curtis reporting his own family as traffic, plus two parents who pass in a doorway, which is my actual life; weakest is a trailer that is four montage images with no complication and no question I could write down.

Strongest is the image of one lit house on a dark grid of forty mailboxes, which no other show owns; weakest is that the pitch is sweeter than it is funny, and a quiet world with tours as the only weekly guest is thin for 100 episodes.

Strongest is Ray writing warnings for things that already happened and Yolanda's scheduled Spontaneous Fun in matching shirts; weakest is that people reading a binder aloud is static on screen and the blended-family category has a famous shadow.

Strongest is five distinct joke engines around a real job at school, with Kwame labeling people like items; weakest is that deadpan and kind is a tone my 11-year-old admires more than laughs at, and the trailer has no turn.

Strongest is Frances, who drives with her ears and is the secret lead every parent will love; weakest is one bus interior twice a day for 100 episodes, which the showrunner admits and the seasons only partly fix.

Strongest is a school where you sit on couches and the mattress department is forbidden, which both my kids would lean into on sight; weakest is that the building is funnier than any kid in it yet, and mattress jokes need watching against soft rule 3.

Strongest is 'Who's in the stands? Our parents,' and a formal debate at halftime, which made me laugh out loud reading it and which a kid can repeat at school; weakest is twelve leads when only three are written.

Strongest is Gus Feeney treating a pickleball schedule like a union contract; weakest is that an 11-year-old will not choose a show about a senior center, and the whole premise is one careless line from an age joke the rules forbid.

Strongest is a premise that escalates by rule, a Code Amber siren for a button, and a tortoise agent who has gained a foot, which a 7-year-old will imitate in the living room; weakest is that an animated animal office is crowded territory and the siren needs a sound-level check.

Strongest is the Rosalind and Docent 4 two-hander, with 'please hold' as a kid laugh on sight; weakest is that an after-hours museum with a night guard sits one step from a famous film premise, and beat 3 of the trailer is montage.

Strongest is a hawk sighting answered by forming a committee while nobody moves; weakest is that a 7-year-old does not know what a quorum is, the show is dialogue over held poses, and parliamentary procedure lives next door to hard rule 8 every single episode.

Strongest is the lost-sock puppets heckling from the bin and a beatboxer who needs the heavy cycle, which is the most imitable thing in the slot; weakest is that variety with no story gives the trailer no unanswered question, so the teaser reads as a sizzle reel the spec forbids.

Strongest is 'That's every week, Harlan, that's how weeks work' and a grandfather and granddaughter who take each other seriously; weakest is a one-joke premise the showrunner already flagged, and the weekly 'no real news' rule is a live wire.

Strongest is Marguerite's desk deadpan, 'Then I'll need two receipts,' which is a last line worth repeating and the exact campfire pleasure the slot wants; weakest is that mundane reveals can feel like cheats unless the clues are fair, and beat 3 is a montage.

Strongest is Benji befriending the fog man, 'He can't stay past sunrise, work thing,' which is the sweet-scared tone exactly; weakest is that a roadside motel with pale guests and a man who thins into the light stands in the shadow of motel horror and wink-vampires, closer to hard rule 7 than the pitch admits.

Strongest is Dot's 'kid with a ghost, ghost with a kid, I panicked,' and Corwin's calm as the safety net; weakest is that it is a radio booth, my 7-year-old needs pictures on a Friday couch, and the showrunner's own fear that it is too gentle to feel spooky is right.

Strongest is the moment before a wrong door opens, a built-in scare every week, and a trailer that lands cold open, turn, and coat-sleeve button cleanly; weakest is a 12-year-old on a bike at strange houses at night, which sits directly on hard rule 6 and needs the mitigation in every scene.

Strongest is the sibling pair, 'It's not a monster, it's a guy, he waved,' which is my two kids exactly, plus a mom with a secret field guide; weakest is that 'it was friendly' is predictable by episode four, and the field-guide card beat uses text cards the trailer spec forbids.
